prompt: Where did Thomas Sowell spend much of his childhood after leaving North Carolina, before later earning a PhD in economics?

choices.text: Harlem, New York City
Chicago's South Side
Atlanta's Sweet Auburn
Washington, D.C.'s Anacostia

explain: Sowell was born in Gastonia, North Carolina, and moved with his family to Harlem as a child. He later served in the Marines, then studied economics at Harvard, Columbia, and the University of Chicago.
source: Hoover Institution fellow profile; A Personal Odyssey

prompt: In A Conflict of Visions, Sowell's constrained vision of human nature is closest to which claim?

choices.text: People are blank slates, so expert planners can redesign society toward moral perfection
Only genetic determinism explains political disagreement
Markets always fail, so unconstrained reason must replace prices
People are limited and self-interested, so politics should emphasize trade-offs, incentives, and institutional checks

explain: The constrained vision treats human nature as imperfect and hard to remake. The unconstrained vision treats people as more malleable and perfectible through articulated reason and elite guidance.
source: A Conflict of Visions (1987), constrained and unconstrained vision

prompt: Sowell's recurring line about policy is best paraphrased as:

choices.text: Good intentions are a sufficient success metric
If voters demand a solution, economics must deliver one
There are no solutions, only trade-offs
Every social problem has one correct technical fix

explain: In the tragic or constrained vision he describes, suffering and scarcity are not abolished by a program. A choice still leaves costs somewhere. The Vision of the Anointed puts it as no solutions in that vision, only trade-offs.
source: A Conflict of Visions; The Vision of the Anointed, discussion of the tragic vision

prompt: In Basic Economics, what does Sowell emphasize as a common result of rent control that keeps rents artificially low?

choices.text: Prices stop mattering because demand no longer responds to price
Housing shortages, waiting lists, and often deterioration of rental stock
Permanent surpluses of brand-new luxury apartments
Construction booms because builders earn more under the cap

explain: Holding price below the market level raises quantity demanded and reduces quantity supplied. Sowell uses wartime and postwar U.S. housing examples among others.
source: Basic Economics, chapters on prices, shortages, and rent control

prompt: What is a central theme of Intellectuals and Society?

choices.text: Idea workers can heavily shape public opinion and policy while facing little personal accountability when ideas fail
Only STEM PhDs should vote
Intellectuals have almost no influence in democracies
Universities should be abolished because books are obsolete

explain: Sowell defines intellectuals as people whose work centers on ideas. He argues they often influence democratic climates of opinion, and he criticizes weak feedback when prescriptions fail empirically.
source: Intellectuals and Society (2009)

prompt: Discrimination and Disparities mainly pushes readers to reject which automatic inference?

choices.text: That discrimination has never existed anywhere
That first-born children never have advantages
That markets always equalize all group averages overnight
That unequal group outcomes by themselves prove discrimination was the sole or primary cause

explain: Sowell argues disparities have many causes, including ones that are not discrimination. Discrimination can matter, but seeing a gap is not enough to infer that only discrimination produced it.
source: Discrimination and Disparities, early chapters on multiple causes of disparities

prompt: In Black Rednecks and White Liberals, Sowell's race-versus-culture theme is closest to which claim?

choices.text: Culture never matters once discrimination is mentioned
Only African history can explain Southern white folkways
Cultural patterns, not race as biology, help explain some group behaviors and outcomes, including traits he traces to Southern redneck culture
Genetics alone determine every social outcome

explain: The title essay argues that some patterns often labeled as uniquely black ghetto culture have historical roots in white Southern cultural patterns, and that romanticizing those patterns can be harmful.
source: Black Rednecks and White Liberals (2005), title essay

prompt: A city caps apartment rents far below market levels to help tenants. Which reaction is most Sowellian?

choices.text: Conclude that demand for housing does not respond to price
Expect shortages, less new rental supply, and pressure to cut maintenance, because price is a signal, not just a number politicians can erase
Assume landlords will build more units once rents are lower
Treat the shortage as proof that rent caps were set too high

explain: Sowell treats prices as conveying scarcities and costs. Cap the price and you do not cancel those realities. You often get queues, deterioration, and reduced supply.
source: Basic Economics, rent control and price controls

prompt: After a factory closes, a panel of professors proposes a detailed national plan for every worker's next job. A Sowellian pushback would most likely stress:

choices.text: The knowledge problem: dispersed local information and changing trade-offs are hard for central planners to know as well as prices and individuals do
That professors always know more than markets about every local job match
That unemployment proves prices convey no useful information
That human nature is unlimited, so one blueprint can optimize everyone's path

explain: Sowell emphasizes that useful knowledge is scattered and that prices help coordinate it. Unconstrained visions overrate articulated elite plans.
source: Basic Economics, prices as signals; Knowledge and Decisions; A Conflict of Visions

prompt: Group A out-earns Group B. An activist says the gap proves discrimination, full stop. Most Sowellian reply?

choices.text: Gaps never matter and need no study
Discrimination is impossible by definition
Only genetics can explain gaps, so stop talking about culture or age
Disparities can have many causes. Discrimination is one possible cause, not an automatic proof from the gap alone

explain: Discrimination and Disparities rejects the leap from unequal outcomes to a single causal story, while still allowing that discrimination can matter.
source: Discrimination and Disparities

prompt: A pundit says a new program will solve poverty with no serious downsides. Which follow-up questions are most in Sowell's spirit?

choices.text: How quickly can we expand it before measuring results?
Which slogan polls best with donors?
Compared to what? At what cost? What hard evidence?
Who feels the most moral about it?

explain: He frames policy as comparative and empirical. A collected version of the three questions asks: compared to what, at what cost, and what are the hard facts? Interviews often say what hard evidence do you have.
source: Ever Wonder Why? and other essays; interviews stating the same three questions

prompt: A celebrated social theory fails in practice, but its academic champions keep promoting it and blame implementation, not the idea. Intellectuals and Society would most likely highlight:

choices.text: That empirical track records are irrelevant to social ideas
Weak accountability: idea workers often face little personal cost when theories produce bad results, so evidence may not revise the vision
That failure proves the theory needed even more funding only
That intellectuals never influence democratic opinion

explain: A core claim is that intellectuals shape climates of opinion yet often are not forced to pay for disastrous prescriptions the way market actors are.
source: Intellectuals and Society

prompt: A reform raises welfare benefits but also sharply reduces the payoff to taking an entry-level job. Sowell's incentives lens most naturally asks:

choices.text: What behavior does this reward, and what unintended responses should we expect?
Only whether the reformers meant well
Whether the slogan mentions justice
Whether experts feel unconstrained by trade-offs

explain: Throughout Basic Economics and his policy writing, he treats incentives as drivers of outcomes, independent of stated goals.
source: Basic Economics, incentives; related policy essays

prompt: Commentators say a minority community's problems must be explained only by race or only by outsider oppression. A Sowellian alternative emphasis would be:

choices.text: Ignore the history of discrimination entirely
Assume all cultures produce identical results under identical laws
Replace cultural discussion with slogans only
Also examine culture, human capital, and internal patterns, not race as destiny and not a single external cause for every gap

explain: Black Rednecks and White Liberals and Discrimination and Disparities stress culture and multiple causes. They reject both a biological destiny story and a discrimination-only story.
source: Black Rednecks and White Liberals; Discrimination and Disparities

prompt: Where and when was Thomas Sowell born?

choices.text: Atlanta, Georgia, on July 4, 1925
Chicago, Illinois, on January 15, 1935
Gastonia, North Carolina, on June 30, 1930
Harlem, New York, on June 30, 1930

explain: He was born in Gastonia during the Depression. His father died before he was born. His mother could not raise him, and his great-aunt Molly did. The move to Harlem came later, in childhood.
source: Hoover Institution fellow profile; Library of Congress name authority (born 1930-06-30, Gastonia, N.C.)

prompt: After he was drafted in 1951, what assignment did the Marine Corps give Sowell?

choices.text: A Navy medical post attached to the Army
Photography, a craft he already cared about
Command of an infantry company in the Pusan Perimeter
Teaching economics at the Naval Academy

explain: Hoover's fellow profile says he was drafted in 1951, during the Korean War, and assigned to photography. He was discharged in 1952. He had not finished high school before that service. He then worked as a civil-service clerk in Washington and took night classes at Howard.
source: Hoover Institution fellow profile; National Endowment for the Humanities medal biography

prompt: Which sequence matches Sowell's economics degrees?

choices.text: Harvard BA, magna cum laude, 1958; Columbia MA, 1959; University of Chicago PhD, 1968
Howard BA, Yale MA, MIT PhD
Columbia BA, Harvard MA, Stanford PhD
UCLA BA, Chicago MA, Harvard PhD

explain: High exam scores and faculty recommendations helped him transfer from night classes at Howard to Harvard. Arthur Burns later recommended him for doctoral study at Chicago, where he worked with George Stigler and Milton Friedman.
source: Hoover Institution profile and fellow profile; Library of Congress name authority

prompt: What was Sowell's University of Chicago doctoral dissertation about?

choices.text: A proof that a minimum wage cannot affect employment
A defense of Soviet central planning
The Phillips curve as a permanent policy menu
A historical analysis of Say's Law

explain: Hoover describes the dissertation as a historical analysis of Say's Law, the classical claim that supplies of goods and services create their own demands. George Stigler was his doctoral advisor.
source: Hoover Institution fellow profile; standard academic biography (doctoral advisor George Stigler)

prompt: Which later post and honors match Sowell's public career?

choices.text: A Supreme Court clerkship, then Attorney General
Poet laureate and chairman of the National Endowment for the Arts
Rose and Milton Friedman Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution, the National Humanities Medal in 2002, and the Bradley Prize in 2003
Nobel Prize in Economics in 1976 and chair of the Federal Reserve

explain: He has been a Hoover senior fellow since 1980. The current title is Rose and Milton Friedman Senior Fellow on Public Policy, Emeritus. The National Humanities Medal (2002) and the Bradley Prize (2003) are separate honors.
source: Hoover Institution profile page

prompt: In Basic Economics, what does Sowell argue a wage floor above the market rate tends to do to less-skilled workers?

choices.text: Remove any trade-off between the wage and the number of jobs
Raise the cost of their labor and reduce the jobs and hours employers offer them
Automatically raise employment because those workers spend more
Affect only workers who already earn far above the floor

explain: He treats a legal wage above what a worker's output is worth to an employer as a price that can leave that worker unemployed or with fewer hours. The argument is about incentives, not about the stated aim of helping low-paid workers.
source: Basic Economics, controlled labor markets and differential impact

prompt: In Applied Economics, what does thinking beyond stage one mean?

choices.text: Following a policy past its first visible effect to the later reactions it sets off
Stopping the analysis at the first group that benefits
Counting only the budget cost in the first year
Preferring whichever policy has the best opening headline

explain: Sowell describes a Harvard class with Arthur Smithies. Sowell stated the first benefit he expected, and Smithies kept asking what would happen after that, until the later effects looked worse than the problem. Most policy talk, he argues, stops at stage one.
source: Applied Economics: Thinking Beyond Stage One, the chapter on one-stage thinking

prompt: Say's Law, the subject of Sowell's Chicago dissertation, is the classical claim that:

choices.text: A legal price floor always raises the quantity demanded
Trade deficits are the only cause of recessions
Demand creates goods even when nothing is produced
Supplies of goods and services create their own demands

explain: Hoover's account of the dissertation uses that gloss: supplies create their own demands. The dissertation itself is a history of the idea, not a claim that modern recessions are impossible.
source: Hoover Institution fellow profile, description of the Chicago dissertation

prompt: What is Affirmative Action Around the World (2004)?

choices.text: A problem set in undergraduate price theory
A novel about campus life at Cornell
Sowell's comparative study of group-preference policies in several countries
A memoir of his years on the Howard faculty

explain: The book looks at preferential policies outside the United States as well as inside it. The quiz question stops at that project. It does not ask you to recite country-by-country results.
source: Affirmative Action Around the World (2004); his wider work on group preferences

prompt: In Sowell's comparative work, a middleman minority is a group that:

choices.text: Is a government board that sets prices between buyers and sellers
Concentrates in trade, retail, or other go-between roles, and often draws hostility out of proportion to its numbers
Is the median voter in a two-party system
Is a racial majority that owns heavy industry

explain: He uses the term for minorities whose economic niche is in the middle of other people's transactions. Overseas trading minorities are the usual examples in that literature. The point is occupational history and the politics around it, not a biological ranking.
source: Sowell's comparative writing on middleman minorities, including Race and Culture and related ethnic studies

prompt: What has Sowell argued about Washington's Dunbar High School, earlier called the M Street School?

choices.text: For decades it met or beat national test norms despite poor funding, and success there cannot be waved off by calling the students middle class without evidence
It was a wealthy boarding school that never enrolled the children of laborers
It opened in 1975 as the nation's first charter school
Its record proves school spending was the only thing that ever mattered

explain: He followed the school from 1870 to 1955. It was renamed Dunbar in 1916. In his telling, 1899 test scores beat two of the city's three white academic high schools, and parent occupations in 1892-93 included many laborers, not a doctor-heavy middle class. Educators who dismissed the record as middle class, he wrote, had not checked.
source: Thomas Sowell, The Education of Minority Children (tsowell.com); Imprimis, January 1999

prompt: What is the job of the papers in Education: Assumptions versus History?

choices.text: Replace history courses with one vocational track for every student
Argue that schools should ignore evidence and follow expert intention
Tell the story of his years as a high-school principal
Test fashionable assumptions about schools and universities against historical and contemporary evidence

explain: The Hoover Institution Press description says the papers test assumptions behind education policies against the record. Topics include affirmative action, race and IQ debates, tuition tax credits, and academic tenure.
source: Hoover Institution Press page for Education: Assumptions versus History

prompt: Late-Talking Children, and the follow-up The Einstein Syndrome, are mainly about:

choices.text: A proposal to delay all reading instruction until age ten
A biography of Einstein's childhood in Ulm
Children who speak late, are often advanced in other ways, and are sometimes mislabeled. Sowell wrote from experience as a parent
A claim that Einstein failed every subject in school

explain: The books describe children who talk late and often show unusual memory, music, or mathematical interest. Sowell's son John was one such child. He reports that the pattern is often mistaken for a broader developmental disorder, including autism.
source: Encyclopedia.com summary of Late-Talking Children; The Einstein Syndrome as the follow-up

prompt: What conclusion does Sowell draw in Charter Schools and Their Enemies (2020)?

choices.text: The book is a novel about a fictional school board
After he matched students by ethnic and economic background, charter students in his comparisons generally did better than students in nearby conventional public schools
Charter schools underperform once family background is mentioned, so he opposes them
Charters and district schools had identical scores in every city he studied

explain: The book is an empirical comparison, not a memoir. Sowell's own presentation is that the charter students in the matched comparisons did better. That is his finding in the book, and critics dispute how far it generalizes.
source: Charter Schools and Their Enemies (2020), as described in contemporary reviews of the book's comparisons

prompt: Sowell left the Cornell faculty in 1969. What reason did he give at the time?

choices.text: Leniency toward black students who were not meeting standards was hurting them, not helping them
Cornell had refused to hire any black faculty
He had been denied tenure for publishing too little
The Marine Corps recalled him to active duty

explain: The New York Times of June 2, 1969, reported his resignation under the headline that leniency hurts blacks. That spring, students seized Willard Straight Hall. He later retold the crisis in the essay The Day Cornell Died. He resigned. He was not fired, and he did not leave to become a university president.
source: New York Times, June 2, 1969; Sowell, The Day Cornell Died (1999)

prompt: Which book is Sowell's broad critique of American schools and universities from the early 1990s?

choices.text: Basic Economics
A Personal Odyssey
The Housing Boom and Bust
Inside American Education

explain: Inside American Education (1993) is the schooling book. Basic Economics is the economics survey, A Personal Odyssey is the memoir, and The Housing Boom and Bust is about housing.
source: Inside American Education (1993)

prompt: How has Sowell treated government wage and price controls?

choices.text: As something that works only when economists oppose it
As a policy he urged President Nixon to adopt
As a recurring temptation that can sound good at first and then produce shortages and other damage
As a tool that ended scarcity both in ancient Rome and in the 1970s

explain: On the National Humanities Medal site he points to Nixon's wage and price controls, which he says sounded good and then failed, and to similar controls under the emperor Diocletian. The example is stage-one appeal versus later damage.
source: National Endowment for the Humanities, National Humanities Medal biography of Thomas Sowell

prompt: Knowledge and Decisions warns that modern society increasingly suffers from which gap?

choices.text: Markets stop conveying information once a society is literate
Decisions are made by people who do not hold the firsthand knowledge those decisions depend on
Too many decisions are left with the people who live with the results
Knowledge is now complete, so a central board can set every price

explain: The 1980 book is about where knowledge sits and where authority sits. Sowell's warning is that the two drift apart, so decisions get made far from the scattered facts that should guide them.
source: Knowledge and Decisions (1980), including the publisher's description of the knowledge gap

prompt: In Basic Economics, how does Sowell connect laws such as the Davis-Bacon Act to black workers?

choices.text: He argues federal wage floors shut out black workers who had been competing by accepting lower pay
He argues Davis-Bacon was written to expand black employment on federal construction
He argues a legal wage floor cannot change who gets hired
He argues the act applied only to farms in Puerto Rico

explain: He groups Davis-Bacon (1931) with the National Industrial Recovery Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act as government wage mandates. His claim is that black workers, who had been employable at market wages, were priced out of jobs after those floors. He also writes that the black unemployment rate was slightly lower than the white rate in 1930 and higher later. That comparison is his, from the book.
source: Basic Economics, differential impact of minimum wages, including Davis-Bacon

prompt: What is Social Justice Fallacies (2023)?

choices.text: A 1975 textbook of input-output tables
The memoir published as A Personal Odyssey
A novel he coauthored with Milton Friedman
Sowell's book on arguments made in the name of social justice

explain: Basic Books published it in 2023. It is a late entry in the same project as his policy books: take claims that travel under a moral label and ask what the evidence and the trade-offs are. This question asks you to identify the book, not to recite a chapter.
source: Social Justice Fallacies (Basic Books, 2023); Hoover Institution profile noting the book

prompt: Which government role does the Library of Congress authority record list for Sowell in 1981?

choices.text: Secretary of Labor
Director of the FBI
A seat on a White House economic advisory board
Chair of the Federal Reserve

prompt: Which book is Sowell's large plain-language survey of economics, as distinct from the memoir and the specialized studies?

choices.text: The Einstein Syndrome
Basic Economics
A Personal Odyssey
Late-Talking Children

No scarcity

Save 1 baby life, lose ~60 other lives, ~$72M
Save 10 babies, lose 10 drivers, ~$720M
No lives changed; only higher fares

prompt: On Three Mile Island, which claim does he make?

Zero died in the “disaster”; two died on the highway fleeing; ~52 lives lost generating replacement power while shut
Nuclear is risk-free in absolute terms
Canoeing is safer than living near any industrial site forever

Driving 10 miles interstate (also ~30 min coal mine / ~6 min canoe)
One commercial flight
A year in a steel mill
